claims.text: The `protect` resource option is a Pulumi-engine construct that is enforced entirely within Pulumi and is never sent to the cloud provider.
Many cloud resources carry their own, separate deletion-protection attributes that the cloud provider enforces independently of anything Pulumi knows about.
GCP Cloud SQL instances have a `deletionProtection` attribute.
AWS RDS instances have a `deletionProtection` attribute.

A resource can be unprotected in Pulumi (i.e., not have the `protect` option set) and still refuse to be deleted due to the cloud provider's own deletion-protection attribute, or vice versa (protected in Pulumi but deletable at the cloud-provider level).

The page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/destroy-failures/#deletion-protection-on-the-resource-itself explains how to distinguish Pulumi's `protect` option from cloud-provider-level deletion protection and how to resolve each.
Pulumi has no single flag to protect every resource in a stack.
Stack transforms can be used to set the `protect` option on every resource as it's registered, achieving protection across the board.

The `protect` resource option guards a resource within Pulumi, but this is distinct from separate deletion-protection attributes that some cloud resources carry, which are enforced independently by the provider or cloud API.
A GCP Cloud SQL instance has a `deletionProtection` attribute enforced by the provider or cloud API, independent of Pulumi's `protect` resource option.
An AWS RDS instance has a `deletionProtection` attribute enforced by the provider or cloud API, independent of Pulumi's `protect` resource option.
Pulumi's `protect` resource option and a cloud resource's own deletion-protection attribute are complementary layers rather than substitutes for one another.

The page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/destroy-failures/#deletion-protection-on-the-resource-itself explains how to distinguish Pulumi's protect option from a resource's own deletion-protection attribute and how to resolve a destroy failure caused by either.
The `retainOnDelete` resource option lets Pulumi remove a resource from state without calling the provider's delete operation, leaving the underlying cloud resource in place.
The `retainOnDelete` resource option takes the opposite approach from `protect`, which refuses to delete a resource.
`retainOnDelete` is the right choice when a user wants to stop managing a resource with Pulumi, or hand it off, without destroying its data.

A `pulumi destroy` failure caused by resource-level deletion protection can stem from one of three distinct layers of protection: Pulumi's own `protect` resource option, a provider-enforced flag, or a cloud-API-enforced protection.
Pulumi's `protect` resource option is an engine-level guard that never reaches the cloud provider.

An error naming a URN and mentioning `protect` indicates the resource is guarded by Pulumi's `protect` resource option, and the fix is documented on the Protect page (/docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/protect/).

Some Pulumi providers refuse to issue the delete call at all when a resource carries a deletion-protection attribute, for example `deletionProtection` on `gcp.sql.DatabaseInstance` or `gcp.container.Cluster`.
When a provider-enforced deletion-protection flag blocks deletion, the failure surfaces from the provider before any request reaches the cloud API.
Some clouds reject the delete call themselves, independent of Pulumi, for example AWS RDS `deletionProtection`, EC2 `disableApiTermination`, or an Azure Resource Manager management lock.
When a cloud-API-enforced protection blocks deletion, the error text comes back from the cloud provider's API, often with a distinct error code such as `ScopeLocked`.
`pulumi destroy` deletes what is already recorded in the stack's state, not what the program currently says.
Setting a deletion-protection attribute to `false` in the Pulumi program is not enough on its own to allow `pulumi destroy` to succeed when provider- or cloud-API-enforced protection is set.

To remove provider- or cloud-API-enforced deletion protection, the correct remediation sequence is: set the deletion-protection attribute to `false` in the Pulumi program, run `pulumi up` so the change reaches both the live resource and Pulumi's state, then run `pulumi destroy`.

If deletion protection was already disabled outside of Pulumi (e.g., directly in the cloud console), running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes the stack's state with reality, and `pulumi destroy` then succeeds without needing an intervening `pulumi up`.
The `gcp.sql.DatabaseInstance` resource has a `deletionProtection` attribute that is provider-enforced.
The `gcp.sql.DatabaseInstance` resource has a nested `settings.deletionProtectionEnabled` attribute that guards the instance at the GCP API level.
The `gcp.container.Cluster` resource has a `deletionProtection` attribute that is provider-enforced.
The `gcp.bigquery.Table` resource has a `deletionProtection` attribute that is provider-enforced.
The `gcp.bigquery.Dataset` resource has a `deleteContentsOnDestroy` attribute, and destroying a dataset that still contains tables fails unless this attribute is set to `true`.
The `aws.rds.Instance` and `aws.rds.Cluster` resources have a `deletionProtection` attribute that is enforced by the AWS API and defaults to `false`.
The `aws.s3.BucketV2` resource has a `forceDestroy` attribute that defaults to `false`, and a non-empty bucket otherwise fails to delete.
The `aws.ec2.Instance` resource has a `disableApiTermination` attribute that is enforced by the AWS API (EC2 termination protection).
The `aws.dynamodb.Table` resource has a `deletionProtectionEnabled` attribute that is enforced by the AWS API and defaults to `false`.

Azure resources under a management lock (`azure-native.authorization.ManagementLockByScope` and scope-specific variants such as `ManagementLockAtResourceLevel`) are enforced by Azure Resource Manager, and a `CanNotDelete` lock must be removed before the resource can be deleted, independent of anything in the Pulumi program.
The `azure-native.keyvault.Vault` resource supports soft delete and purge protection, and destroying the vault only soft-deletes it.

Recreating an Azure Key Vault with the same name fails with `VaultAlreadyExists` until the soft-deleted vault is purged or recovered, and purge protection prevents purging until its retention period elapses.
